messages.content: everything coming out of the dryer lately has crazy static cling, socks stuck to shirts, the works. it's gotten worse recently

Static usually gets worse in colder, drier weather/seasons since low humidity increases static buildup, so if it's ramped up recently that timing might line up. Overdrying is another big contributor, running the dryer longer than needed strips too much moisture and increases static, try pulling clothes out slightly damp or using a shorter cycle. Dryer balls (wool or even just a couple of clean tennis balls) help by keeping items separated so they generate less friction against each other.
do dryer sheets actually work or is that a myth

They genuinely work, not a myth, dryer sheets coat fabric with a thin layer of fabric softener/lubricant that reduces friction and neutralizes the static charge as clothes tumble. If you don't have any on hand, a crumpled ball of aluminum foil tossed in with the load is a commonly used substitute that works via a similar static-dissipating mechanism, though dryer sheets tend to be a bit more consistently effective and also add scent/softness as a bonus.
I'm a beginner at chess. what are the actual principles behind good opening play, not just memorizing lines?

Three big ideas cover most of it. First, control the center - pawns and pieces that influence the central squares give you more space and flexibility for your pieces to maneuver. Second, develop your minor pieces before moving the same piece twice or bringing your queen out early - wasting tempo lets your opponent develop faster and seize initiative. Third, castle reasonably early to get your king to safety and connect your rooks, unless there's a concrete tactical reason to delay it. A lot of beginner mistakes come from ignoring one of these - like pushing too many pawns without developing pieces, or chasing a pawn grab with the queen while your opponent develops three pieces and starts attacking.
is it bad to develop knights before bishops or does it not matter

There's a mild general guideline of knights before bishops, mainly because a knight's best square is often clear early, whereas a bishop's ideal diagonal can depend on how the pawn structure develops, so committing it too early can mean redeploying it later. But it's a soft guideline, not a rule - plenty of strong openings develop a bishop first when there's a clear good square, like a fianchetto setup you want to get to early.
where does the word salary actually come from? I heard something about salt

That's a popular etymology and it's mostly right, though the details get exaggerated sometimes. Salary comes from Latin salarium, which is tied to sal, meaning salt. The common story is that Roman soldiers were paid in salt because it was valuable for preserving food, but most historians now think it's more likely that salarium referred to an allowance given to soldiers specifically to buy salt, rather than salt itself being handed over as payment. Salt was indeed a valuable commodity in the ancient world - used for preservation, trade, and even religious rituals - so the connection between wages and salt makes sense even if the literal paid-in-salt version is probably folk etymology layered on top of a real linguistic root.
is salad related too then?

Yes, actually - salad traces back to the Latin herba salata, meaning salted vegetables, since Romans commonly seasoned raw greens with a brine or salt dressing. That passed through Old French salade before entering English. So salary and salad are etymological cousins, both rooted in sal, even though they ended up describing completely unrelated things in modern usage.

My alma mater has this massive endowment, in the billions, and yet they're always doing fundraising drives for basic stuff. Why don't they just spend more of the endowment every year instead of constantly asking alumni for more money?

It feels counterintuitive, but there's a deliberate structural reason behind it, and it's similar in spirit to how a company manages a long-term payout it wants to sustain indefinitely rather than draw down. Most university endowments operate under a spending policy that intentionally caps annual withdrawals at a modest percentage of the fund's value, commonly somewhere in the range of four to five percent, specifically because the goal is for the endowment to exist in perpetuity, supporting the institution not just this year but a century from now, adjusted for whatever inflation and growth happens along the way. If a university spent a much larger share every year, it would boost funding in the short term but would shrink the real, inflation-adjusted value of the endowment over time, eventually leaving future students and faculty with a much smaller cushion than current ones enjoy, which conflicts with the whole premise of an endowment as an intergenerational resource rather than a one-time windfall to be consumed.
Okay that makes sense for the endowment itself, but then why do the ongoing fundraising drives feel disconnected from that, like they're going after totally different pots of money?

They largely are different pots, and that's actually the source of the disconnect you're noticing. The endowment's restrained annual spending typically covers a defined, recurring slice of the university's budget, things like a portion of financial aid, endowed faculty chairs, maintenance of specific funds donors set up for particular purposes, often with legal restrictions on exactly what that money can be used for, since many large gifts come with donor-specified conditions attached rather than being free for the university to spend however it wants. Ongoing fundraising drives, by contrast, are usually targeting new capital projects, a new building, a new program, or unrestricted operating funds the university can deploy flexibly for whatever current needs arise, which the endowment's restricted, conservatively managed structure isn't well suited to cover. So it's less that the university is being stingy with a giant pile of cash sitting around, and more that most of that pile is legally earmarked or structurally protected for specific long-term purposes, leaving a real ongoing need for fresh, flexible money.
That's actually a much more sympathetic picture than I had going in. Does the same restrained-payout logic apply to like, family trusts and inheritance funds too, or is that a totally separate thing?

The underlying principle genuinely does show up in family trusts as well, and it's really the same core tension, balancing current beneficiaries' desire for income now against preserving the fund's real value for future beneficiaries or generations. Trust documents very often specify a payout rate or formula for exactly this reason, to prevent a current beneficiary from draining the principal and leaving nothing for whoever comes after them, and trustees have a formal fiduciary duty to balance those competing interests rather than simply favoring whoever is asking loudest in the present moment. The specific percentages and mechanisms differ, and family trusts have a lot more variety in structure since they're privately negotiated documents rather than following a fairly standardized nonprofit convention, but the philosophical throughline, protecting a fund's ability to keep supporting people indefinitely rather than treating it as a spendable lump sum, is essentially the same idea showing up in a more personal, family-scale context.

why do my succulents keep dying, I water them all the time to be safe

That's actually the problem, succulents store water in their leaves and are adapted to dry, infrequent watering, so "watering a lot to be safe" is the opposite of what they need. Overwatering leads to root rot, which often looks like mushy, translucent, or yellowing leaves, easy to mistake for underwatering at first glance which makes people water even more.
how often should I actually be watering them then

Depends on the species and pot/soil, but a good general approach is to let the soil dry out completely between waterings, then water thoroughly until it drains out the bottom. In most homes that ends up being every 2-3 weeks, sometimes longer in winter when they're semi-dormant. Stick a finger in the soil before watering rather than following a fixed schedule, and make sure the pot has drainage holes since standing water is what actually causes the rot.
Every few months the news just becomes wall to wall coverage of some big tech company's earnings, and it always seems way more dramatic than it needs to be.

Yeah earnings season definitely has a theatrical quality to it, especially for the handful of companies that move markets broadly. Do you find yourself actually following it, or is it more background noise you can't avoid?
Mostly background noise, but it's funny how a stock can drop a bunch even when the company technically made more money than before.

That happens a lot and it trips people up who assume good results should always mean a rising stock. A lot of the reaction is less about the raw numbers and more about whether those numbers matched or missed what investors were already expecting going in, plus whatever guidance the company gives about the road ahead. A company can post record profits and still see its stock fall if the market had priced in even rosier expectations or didn't like something in the forward-looking commentary. It's a good reminder that markets are reacting to surprise relative to expectations, not just to the raw headline numbers themselves.
organizing our office gift exchange this year, want to set a good price limit and rules, last year got kind of awkward

Sorry last year was rough, happy to help set this up cleaner. A common sweet spot for price limit is $20-25, enough to get something decent without anyone feeling pressured to overspend or embarrassed by a cheap-feeling gift. Clear rules that help avoid awkwardness: set a specific theme or category (funny gifts only, something under $X, a specific niche like 'office supplies but make it fun') so people aren't guessing what's appropriate. A White Elephant or Yankee Swap format (where people can steal gifts) tends to keep energy fun and light rather than a straightforward one-to-one gift exchange which can feel more personal and prone to comparison.
we tried a straight name draw last year and someone felt like their gift was way worse than others, that's what went wrong

That's exactly the failure mode a swap-style format solves, since gift quality comparison becomes part of the fun (people fighting over the good gift) rather than a sore point tied to one specific person's gift-giving. I'd switch to White Elephant this year: everyone brings one wrapped gift within your price limit, people take turns either picking a new wrapped gift or 'stealing' an already-opened one from someone else (usually capped at 2-3 steals per gift to keep it moving), and it ends naturally once everyone's had a turn. It depersonalizes the process since nobody's gift is tied to being 'from' a specific person in an awkward comparison sense, and the stealing mechanic usually gets genuine laughs rather than quiet disappointment.

I'm seriously considering going back for an MBA specifically to pivot into a corporate finance role at a mid-size company, like FP&A or treasury type stuff. Is that a reasonable path or overkill for that kind of job?

It really depends on where you're starting from and how far you want to climb, not just the target job title. For an entry or mid-level FP&A or treasury analyst role at a mid-size company, plenty of people get in and advance without an MBA, especially if they already have relevant experience, an accounting background, or a professional certification along those lines. Where an MBA tends to earn its cost back is less about the specific FP&A analyst job itself and more about the ceiling above it, moving into a director of finance or eventually a CFO-track role often benefits from the broader strategic and cross-functional exposure an MBA program provides, plus the network, which matters a lot for those higher-level jumps. If your target really is capped at a solid individual-contributor or manager level in corporate finance, the MBA is probably more expensive insurance than you need.
What would actually make more sense instead if I'm not trying to become a CFO someday, just want a stable senior analyst or manager role?

For that ceiling, a professional certification is usually a much more cost-effective credential than a full MBA, since it signals technical competence directly relevant to the job without the two years and often six-figure cost of a full-time program. Depending on which corner of corporate finance you're aiming at, that might mean something oriented toward accounting and financial reporting rigor, or something more oriented toward investment and capital markets knowledge if you're leaning treasury. Beyond the credential itself, direct experience tends to matter more than either, getting into an FP&A-adjacent role even at a junior level, like a financial analyst position in an operations or accounting department, and building a track record of solid work there usually opens the internal path upward faster than an outside credential would on its own. Companies promoting into these mid-level finance roles usually care more about demonstrated judgment on real numbers than about pedigree.

That's reassuring honestly, I was dreading the idea of quitting my job for two years. One more thing, does the industry matter a lot, like would finance experience at a tech company transfer well to, say, manufacturing?

The core skills transfer better than people expect, but there are real differences in emphasis that are worth being upfront about in interviews rather than pretending they don't exist. Tech company finance roles tend to be heavier on modeling growth and unit economics, subscription metrics, customer acquisition costs, that sort of thing, while manufacturing finance leans more on cost accounting, inventory and working capital management, and capital expenditure planning for physical assets. The underlying analytical muscle, building models, communicating findings to non-finance stakeholders, understanding how operational decisions flow through to the financials, is genuinely transferable. What you'd want to do in an interview is acknowledge the different emphasis honestly and point to the parts of your background that map most directly, rather than assuming the interviewer will just take the transfer for granted, since some hiring managers in more traditional industries can be a little skeptical of finance folks coming from tech.

My work book club wants to read something business-related next and someone suggested a book about how companies scale from startup to big corporation. Any general advice on what makes those books actually good versus just fluffy success-story stuff?

The good ones tend to share a few traits regardless of which company they're about. First, they show the messy middle, the awkward years where the founders were making decisions with incomplete information and no idea if they'd work, rather than jumping straight from 'garage idea' to 'market leader' with the hard part glossed over. Second, they include the failures and near-death moments honestly, a scaling story with zero setbacks is almost always sanitized. Third, the best ones explain the actual mechanics of how a company's priorities change as it grows, how a ten-person team making gut calls has to become a thousand-person organization with processes, and that transition is usually where the most interesting tension lives. Books that focus purely on the charismatic founder narrative and skip that operational reality tend to be the fluffier ones.
That's helpful. What kinds of discussion questions would actually get people talking instead of just summarizing the plot of the book?

Steer away from 'what happened' questions and toward 'would this apply to us' questions, since your group presumably works somewhere with its own scaling pains, even if it's a much smaller company. Something like: at what point did the company in the book have to trade speed for structure, and does that match a moment you've seen at your own workplace? Or: which decision in the book do you think was actually lucky rather than strategic, dressed up in hindsight as a brilliant call? Another good one is asking people to identify the moment the culture of the company visibly shifted, and whether they think that shift was necessary or a loss. Personal-experience questions like these generate way more conversation than anything that can be answered by just recalling a chapter.
Good point. Should we also try to pick a book about a company that eventually failed, for balance, or keep it upbeat?

I'd actually lean toward including a failure story, or at least a company that had a serious near-collapse before recovering, because those books tend to generate the richest discussion. Success stories can lull a reading group into treating every decision the founders made as obviously correct in hindsight, when in reality most of it was uncertain at the time. A failure narrative forces everyone to sit with the discomfort of 'this looked like a smart choice and it still didn't work,' which is a much more realistic lesson about how much luck and timing matter versus pure strategy. If you want to keep morale up, you could pair a partial-failure story with a recovery arc, so the group leaves with something instructive rather than purely cautionary.

I've been reading about determinism and free will and it's honestly making me feel weirdly anxious, like if everything is predetermined then nothing I do matters. Can you help me actually understand the different positions here, not just the scary version I've been spiraling about?

That anxious spiral is a really common reaction to first encountering hard determinism specifically, and it's worth knowing upfront that the "nothing matters" conclusion isn't actually where most serious philosophical positions on this land, even among philosophers who accept determinism, so let's walk through the actual landscape rather than just the one alarming conclusion. Hard determinism holds that every event, including every human decision, is the necessary result of prior causes, given the state of the universe and its laws, only one outcome was ever possible, meaning free will in the sense of "could have done otherwise" is an illusion. This is the position that tends to trigger the anxiety you're describing. But there are two other major positions worth knowing. Libertarian free will (unrelated to the political term) holds that genuine free will exists and is incompatible with determinism being fully true, that at the moment of choice there's a real, undetermined branching point where you could have chosen otherwise, this is closer to the intuitive, everyday feeling of choice most people have. The position most professional philosophers actually hold, according to surveys of philosophers, is compatibilism, which argues that free will and determinism aren't actually in conflict at all, free will isn't about being uncaused, it's about acting according to your own reasons, desires, and values without external coercion, under this view, a decision being caused by your character, history, and reasoning is exactly what free will consists of, not something that undermines it, since the alternative, a decision caused by nothing at all, random rather than determined, wouldn't feel more free, it would just feel arbitrary.

The compatibilist view is interesting but I'm still not sure I get how it actually resolves the anxiety. Like even if my choices come from my own character, that character itself was determined by things I didn't choose, genes, upbringing, etc. Doesn't that just push the problem back a step?

That's a genuinely sharp objection and it's actually one of the most discussed challenges to compatibilism in the literature, sometimes called the "disappearing agent" or manipulation argument, so you're not missing something obvious, you've found a real fault line in the position rather than a naive gap. Compatibilists have a few responses worth knowing. One is that the objection assumes free will requires being the ultimate, uncaused source of your own character, but that standard is arguably incoherent even in principle, since literally nothing, free or not, could meet a standard of being self-caused from absolute scratch with zero prior influence, that's not a special problem for determinism, it's just what causation is, so holding free will to that impossible standard means nothing could ever count as free will under any metaphysics whatsoever, determined or not. A different, and honestly more practically useful, response reframes the whole question: rather than asking "could I have done otherwise given the exact same universe," which may be genuinely unanswerable and perhaps even meaningless, ask a more functional question, "am I the kind of system that responds to reasons, that changes behavior when given new information or reflection, that isn't being externally coerced," and by that standard, which is arguably what actually matters for holding people responsible, praising them, and for your own sense of agency day to day, you clearly do qualify, regardless of the deeper metaphysical question about ultimate origins. On the anxiety specifically, it might help to notice that this deeper question, however it resolves, changes literally nothing about your actual lived experience of deliberating, weighing options, and choosing, the phenomenology of choice remains identical either way, and most philosophers who've thought hardest about this, including committed hard determinists, report living completely normal lives with normal senses of purpose and responsibility, the abstract metaphysical fact, whichever it turns out to be, simply doesn't cash out into the lived meaninglessness that the initial spiral suggests it would.
quick german question - is there a real difference between "kennen" and "wissen" or are they basically the same as "to know"?

Real difference, not interchangeable. "Kennen" is for knowing/being familiar with a person, place, or thing through direct acquaintance — "Ich kenne diese Stadt" (I know/am familiar with this city), "Ich kenne ihn" (I know him). "Wissen" is for knowing facts or information — "Ich weiß, dass er kommt" (I know that he's coming), "Ich weiß die Antwort" (I know the answer). Rough rule: if you could rephrase the English sentence as 'I'm familiar with X,' use kennen; if it's 'I know that / I know a fact,' use wissen. English collapses both into 'know,' which is why it trips people up.

I've been doing Duolingo for Spanish for 6 months and I feel like I know a lot of words but can't actually hold a conversation. What am I missing?

This is an extremely common gap and it's not really about vocabulary size, it's that apps like Duolingo train recognition and translation in isolated sentences, which is a different skill from real-time production under conversational pressure, where you need to retrieve grammar and vocabulary quickly while also listening and responding, with no time to think through conjugation rules. The fix is deliberately practicing output under time pressure rather than more input accumulation. A few concrete changes: start doing italki or similar tutoring sessions, even just 30 minutes a week with a conversation-focused tutor, since nothing replicates the pressure and unpredictability of real conversation like an actual conversation, apps simply can't simulate the need to formulate a response in real time to something you didn't expect. Second, practice thinking in Spanish during small daily moments, narrating your actions internally in simple Spanish while making coffee or driving, which builds the retrieval speed that conversation requires without needing a partner every time. Third, shift some study time from vocabulary apps to listening to native content at a slightly-too-hard level, podcasts or shows with Spanish subtitles, since comprehension speed is often the bigger bottleneck than production, you can't respond to something you're still mentally translating word by word.
I'm nervous about the tutoring thing, I feel like I'll freeze up and embarrass myself. Any tips for getting over that?

That fear is nearly universal among learners at your stage and it's worth naming directly to a tutor at the start of your first session, something like "I'm nervous and I know I'll make mistakes, please be patient with me," which immediately changes the dynamic since a good tutor will slow down and reassure you rather than you silently panicking while they wonder why you've gone quiet. A few practical tricks beyond that: request a tutor who explicitly works with beginners or nervous students, most platforms let you filter or read reviews for this, and book your first session with a clear, low-stakes topic prepared in advance, like introducing yourself, your daily routine, or your hobbies, so you're not being asked fully open-ended questions with zero preparation. It also helps enormously to accept in advance that freezing up and needing a moment is completely normal and expected, not a sign you're bad at this, even fluent second-language speakers pause mid-sentence, and a decent tutor is used to sitting through silences without judgment. Consider also starting with text-based conversation practice, like a language exchange app with voice messages instead of live calls, as a stepping stone, since it removes the real-time pressure while still forcing you to produce language rather than just recognize it, then graduate to live tutoring once that feels more comfortable. The freeze-up feeling reliably fades within just a handful of sessions once your brain gets used to the format.

I keep getting confused about the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN in SQL. I understand them individually when I look them up but I can't seem to keep it straight when actually writing queries. Any way to make this click permanently?

The stickiest way to internalize this is a visual/set mental model rather than memorizing definitions, since the definitions themselves are what keeps slipping out of memory. Picture two overlapping circles, a Venn diagram, one circle for table A, one for table B, overlapping in the middle where rows match on your join condition. INNER JOIN returns only the overlapping middle section, rows that have a match in both tables, anything in either table without a match on the other side is simply dropped entirely, gone from the result. LEFT JOIN returns the entire left circle, all of table A no matter what, plus the overlapping middle where matches exist, but where table A has no match in table B, those columns from B just show up as NULL rather than the row being dropped, this is the key difference from inner join, nothing from the left table ever disappears. FULL OUTER JOIN returns the entire combined area of both circles, everything from A, everything from B, with NULLs filling in wherever a match doesn't exist on the other side, so unlike inner join, nothing from either table is ever dropped. A memory trick that helps a lot of people: with LEFT JOIN, read it as "give me everything from the left table, and whatever matches from the right, it's fine if there's nothing on the right." That plain English framing tends to stick better than the Venn diagram alone once you pair the two together.
That helps. When would I actually want a LEFT JOIN over an INNER JOIN in a real scenario, not just conceptually?

The real world signal for choosing LEFT JOIN over INNER JOIN is whenever the absence of a match is itself meaningful information you want to see in your results, rather than something you're fine silently discarding. A classic example: imagine a customers table and an orders table, and you want a report of all customers along with their most recent order. If you use INNER JOIN, any customer who has never placed an order simply vanishes from your results entirely, which is a problem if your actual goal was something like "show me all customers, including ones who haven't ordered yet, so marketing can target them with a promotion." A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders keeps every customer in the result regardless of whether they have orders, with NULL values in the order columns for customers with no orders, which you can then filter for directly, like WHERE order_id IS NULL, to specifically identify customers who've never purchased anything, a query that's structurally impossible to write correctly using INNER JOIN since those rows wouldn't exist in an inner-joined result to filter in the first place. As a general rule of thumb: use INNER JOIN when you only care about complete, matched records, like a sales report that only makes sense for actual transactions that happened, and reach for LEFT JOIN whenever one side of the relationship is your "primary" entity you want fully preserved regardless of whether a related record exists, like customers, employees, or products where the absence of related activity is meaningful business information.

A good approach is usually to lean on a really concrete, almost silly example before getting abstract, like the old story about folding a piece of paper in half enough times that it would theoretically reach the moon, it captures how slow growth in the early stages hides how dramatic it becomes later. Pairing that with a simple visual, like a line that looks flat for a while and then curves sharply upward, tends to land better than just describing the math in words.

Framing your post around 'here's a rough rule you can use at a dinner party, and here's the intuition behind why it works' is usually more memorable than a purely formal explanation.

tried making bread for the first time and the dough just did not rise at all after an hour. what went wrong

Most likely culprit is the yeast, either it was dead/expired, or the water used to activate it was too hot (above roughly 120F/49C kills yeast) or too cold to activate it well. Another common issue is not enough time or too cold a room, an hour might just not be enough if your kitchen is on the cooler side, rising can take 1.5-2+ hours in a cold room.
how do I test if my yeast is actually still good before I waste another batch

Easy test: dissolve a teaspoon of sugar in about half a cup of warm water (around 105-110F, warm to the touch but not hot), sprinkle a packet or a tablespoon of yeast on top, and wait 5-10 minutes. If it gets foamy and bubbly, it's alive and good to use. If nothing happens after 10 minutes, the yeast is dead and you'll need a fresh batch before trying the bread again, no point troubleshooting anything else in the recipe until that's confirmed good.
switched my cat to a new food brand and she's basically refusing to eat it, just sniffs and walks away. is this normal

Very normal, cats are notoriously picky about food transitions, partly texture/smell sensitivity and partly just neophobia. A cold-turkey switch is the most common cause of this reaction. Try mixing a small amount of the new food in with the old, like 25% new / 75% old, and gradually shift the ratio over 7-10 days. Also check if the new food's texture (pate vs shreds vs chunks) is really different from what she's used to, that matters more than flavor sometimes.
she's already refused it for 2 days straight, should i be worried

2 days of reduced eating from pickiness alone usually isn't dangerous for an adult cat, but if she's eating literally nothing (not even treats or the old food) past 24-48 hours, that's worth calling a vet about, since cats can develop a liver issue called hepatic lipidosis if they go too long without any food. If she'll still eat the old brand, just go back to that for now and reintroduce the new one more slowly later, no need to force it this week.

I used to manage a little diner in college and I still think about how agonizing it was every time we had to raise menu prices. Owner would sit there for like an hour debating whether to bump the burger from 8.50 to 9 or just go straight to 9.50. Did we way overthink that?

Honestly, for a small independent place, that hour of agonizing was probably time well spent, even if it felt absurd in the moment. Menu pricing on a handful of signature items acts almost like a mood-setter for the whole menu, customers anchor their sense of 'is this place fair' on the two or three dishes they order most, like the burger. A 50-cent jump can read as normal inflation creep, but going straight to a full dollar risks crossing a psychological threshold, especially if it pushes past a round number people mentally associate with a price tier. Chains run this through data across hundreds of locations, but a single diner owner is essentially doing the same instinct-driven version with much less to go on, so the hand-wringing was really a stand-in for market research he couldn't otherwise afford.
We ended up doing 9.25 as some weird compromise. In hindsight was that a cop-out?

It's not a cop-out so much as a classic 'anchor between two options' move, which is actually a legitimate approach when you don't have great data. Splitting the difference avoids the two failure modes he was worried about: looking greedy with a full dollar jump, or looking indecisive by doing another small bump again in three months. The odd number, 9.25, also has a side benefit of feeling more 'calculated' than a round or half number, some diners subconsciously read precise pricing as more deliberate and less like a lazy across-the-board increase. The real test isn't whether the number was theoretically optimal, it's whether regulars grumbled and stopped ordering it, or just paid it without comment. If nobody complained and the burger kept selling at the same volume, the price was fine regardless of how it was arrived at.
Nobody said a word actually. We were more worried about it than we needed to be I think.

That's usually how it goes with small, well-loved local spots. Regulars have a lot more price tolerance for a place they already trust than owners give them credit for, especially when the increase tracks roughly with what they're seeing everywhere else, gas, groceries, other restaurants. The bigger risk is usually not raising prices often enough and then having to do one jarring double-digit jump later because costs quietly outpaced revenue for two years straight. Small, semi-frequent adjustments like yours are much easier for customers to absorb without noticing, even if they're nerve-wracking for the person making the call in the moment.

my kitchen table has had a wobbly leg for months, one corner just doesn't sit flush. easy fix or do I need a new table

brainstorming a villain for my fantasy novel. i want someone who isn't evil for evil's sake, more like tragic but still does bad things. any archetypes to consider?

A few well-worn but flexible archetypes for that: the reformer who becomes what they fought (started trying to fix a corrupt system, adopted its methods, lost themselves), the griever (lost someone and their solution to grief becomes destructive to others — necromancy, forbidden magic, vengeance), the loyalist (utterly devoted to a cause or person that turns out to be rotten, and their tragedy is not realizing it, or realizing too late), and the pragmatist (genuinely believes the ends justify the means and is proven partly right, which is more unsettling than a villain who's simply wrong). The griever and the loyalist tend to generate the most reader sympathy because their logic is emotionally legible even when the actions are monstrous. Reformer-turned-tyrant works well if you want a mirror to your protagonist.
I like the loyalist idea. What's a good way to show the moment they realize the cause is rotten, without it feeling like a sudden flip?

Don't make it one moment — build a string of small, deniable ones first. A cruel order they rationalize, a person they trusted lying to their face, a result that technically worked but felt wrong in the room. The realization scene itself should land on something small and specific rather than a grand revelation — a villain seeing, say, a child's shoe left behind after an operation they authorized, rather than being told 'the cause was evil all along.' The gap between the abstract justification they've repeated for years and one ungeneralizable, human detail is usually what breaks people in fiction (and in life). Let them still try to rationalize it once more before it fails to hold.

quick grammar q: "I like dogs, cats, and birds" vs "I like dogs, cats and birds" — is the oxford comma actually required or just style?

It's style, not a hard grammatical requirement — both are considered correct English, and which one is 'right' depends on the style guide you're following. AP style (common in journalism) drops the oxford comma except when needed for clarity. Chicago Manual of Style, and most academic/book publishing, requires it. The strongest case FOR always using it is that it avoids genuine ambiguity in some sentences — the classic example being "I'd like to thank my parents, Ayn Rand and God" (no oxford comma) versus "I'd like to thank my parents, Ayn Rand, and God" (with it) — the first reads as if your parents are Ayn Rand and God. So even AP-style writers usually add it when a sentence would otherwise misparse. For everyday writing, either is fine as long as you're consistent throughout the piece.
why did linear perspective specifically emerge in renaissance italy? was nobody drawing depth before that?

Artists before the Renaissance absolutely tried to convey depth, but earlier techniques like overlapping figures, varying size somewhat intuitively, or medieval hierarchical scaling, where important figures like saints were drawn larger regardless of actual distance, weren't built on a consistent mathematical system. Linear perspective as a systematic, geometrically grounded technique is usually credited to the architect Filippo Brunelleschi in early 15th century Florence, who demonstrated that a scene's depth could be constructed by having parallel lines converge toward a single vanishing point on the horizon, mirroring how the eye actually perceives receding parallel lines like a road or a row of columns. Leon Battista Alberti then formalized this into a written treatise, giving other artists a reproducible method rather than an intuitive trick. It emerged specifically in Renaissance Florence partly because of the era's broader intellectual climate blending art with mathematics and optics, revived interest in classical Greek and Roman ideas about geometry, and patronage from wealthy families and guilds eager to fund ambitious architectural and artistic projects that rewarded this kind of technical innovation.
did that mathematical approach change how artists were trained after that, or was it more of a niche technique some used?

It became foundational fairly quickly, at least in Italy and then across Europe. Once linear perspective was formalized, it got incorporated into workshop training as a core technical skill alongside anatomy and proportion, since it gave artists a reliable method for constructing believable architectural spaces and figure placement rather than relying purely on instinct. Within a couple of generations it was assumed knowledge for any ambitious painter, and treatises on perspective, proportion, and anatomy became standard parts of an artist's theoretical education, reflecting the Renaissance ideal of the artist as someone versed in both craft and scientific principles rather than purely a manual craftsman.
what's the actual chemical difference between the fermentation that makes beer alcoholic and the one that makes yogurt sour?

They're driven by completely different organisms producing different end products from the same starting sugar. Beer fermentation is alcoholic fermentation, carried out by yeast, typically Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide through glycolysis followed by the enzyme pathway that reduces pyruvate to acetaldehyde and then to ethanol, regenerating NAD+ in the process so glycolysis can keep running without oxygen. Yogurt fermentation is lactic acid fermentation, carried out by bacteria like Lactobacillus and Streptococcus thermophilus, which convert the lactose sugar in milk into lactic acid, again regenerating NAD+ but through a different single-step reduction of pyruvate directly to lactate rather than the two-step pathway to ethanol. The lactic acid buildup is what curdles the milk proteins and gives yogurt its characteristic tang, while in beer the ethanol and CO2 are the defining products, with the CO2 also responsible for carbonation if it's trapped during fermentation.
why does muscle tissue also do lactic acid fermentation during hard exercise then, is it using bacteria?

No bacteria involved there - it's your own muscle cells running the same basic anaerobic fallback pathway, just without any microorganisms. When oxygen supply can't keep up with ATP demand during intense exercise, muscle cells can't run oxidative phosphorylation fast enough, so they shift to anaerobic glycolysis, and just like in the yogurt bacteria, they need to regenerate NAD+ to keep glycolysis running, which they do by converting pyruvate into lactate via the same type of enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase. It's essentially the same core biochemical solution to the same underlying problem, run independently by two very different kinds of cells that both need to keep glycolysis functioning without oxygen.

I was reading a bit about Warren Buffett and it struck me as ironic that Berkshire Hathaway itself doesn't pay a dividend even though he's famous for investing in companies that do. What's the actual reasoning there?

It's not really a contradiction once you understand the logic he's articulated over the decades, and it actually follows a pretty consistent internal principle rather than being an inconsistency. His stated position is that a company should only retain earnings rather than pay them out if management can reinvest that capital at a better rate of return than shareholders could achieve on their own by taking the cash and investing it elsewhere. Berkshire's argument for not paying a dividend is essentially a claim that Buffett and his team can find better uses for the retained capital, acquiring whole businesses, buying stakes in undervalued companies, than the average shareholder could manage independently with that same cash in hand. When he invests in other companies that do pay dividends, it's not inconsistent with that principle, it's actually the flip side of the same logic, he's implicitly judging that those companies can't reinvest all their earnings at an attractive enough rate, so returning some cash to shareholders, including Berkshire itself as a shareholder, is the better move for those specific businesses.

So basically he's saying 'trust me more than you trust yourself with this money, but I don't extend that same trust to those other companies'? That feels a little self-serving when you put it that way.

It's a fair thing to be skeptical of in principle, since almost every executive who avoids paying dividends could make some version of that same claim about being a better allocator of capital than their shareholders, and plenty of them are wrong about it. What makes Buffett's specific version more credible, rather than just self-serving rhetoric, is the multi-decade track record actually backing the claim, Berkshire's compounded returns over a very long stretch have genuinely outpaced what a typical shareholder would likely have achieved reinvesting dividend cash on their own, so it's a claim that's been repeatedly tested against reality rather than just asserted. The honest caveat he's given himself is that this logic has a shelf life, he's been fairly candid in shareholder letters that as Berkshire has grown enormous, finding new opportunities large enough to meaningfully move the needle has gotten harder, which is an implicit acknowledgment that the same no-dividend argument gets weaker as the pool of retained capital grows relative to the available high-return opportunities.
That's a fair distinction actually, track record versus just asserting it. Do you think Berkshire will eventually have to start paying one once Buffett isn't running it?

It's a reasonable prediction, and quite a few observers of the company have floated it for similar reasons. The no-dividend policy has always been sustainable specifically because there was strong confidence in the capital allocator's ability to keep finding attractive uses for the cash, and that confidence was built directly on Buffett's individual track record and reputation over an extraordinarily long career. Once leadership transitions to whoever succeeds him, even a highly capable successor, that same level of accumulated trust doesn't transfer automatically, it has to be earned freshly, and in the meantime shareholders and the market may be less patient about large amounts of cash sitting retained without a similarly storied allocator at the helm to justify it. That dynamic, more than any change in the underlying financial logic, is probably what would eventually push a future Berkshire toward returning cash directly to shareholders, not because the reinvestment principle stopped being sound in theory, but because the specific trust that made it credible in practice was personal to one person's results.

What were the main structural reasons the Roman Republic collapsed, beyond just Caesar crossing the Rubicon?

The Rubicon moment was really the culmination of decades of structural strain rather than a sudden cause. A few big threads: first, the Republic's institutions were designed for a city-state, not the sprawling Mediterranean empire Rome had become by the 2nd century BCE - governors and generals far from Rome accumulated personal power and loyal armies that owed more to them than to the state. Second, the Marian reforms professionalized the army and tied soldiers' loyalty to their commanders, who promised land and pay, rather than to the Senate - this made generals like Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar into independent power brokers with private armies. Third, growing economic inequality - cheap slave labor from conquests undercut small farmers, who lost land and flooded into Rome, creating a volatile urban poor that populist politicians could mobilize. Finally, the Senate's own conservatism and unwillingness to reform (the failed attempts by the Gracchi brothers to redistribute land are a good example) meant grievances built up with no institutional outlet, so they got resolved through violence and civil war instead.
did the Gracchi reforms actually have a chance of working if the Senate hadn't blocked them?

Hard to say definitively, but many historians think a version of the reforms could have relieved some pressure - redistributing public land that wealthy senators had informally monopolized might have slowed the decline of the small farmer class that fed the legions. But the deeper structural issues, like provincial governance and army loyalty, wouldn't have been touched by land reform alone, so it likely would have delayed rather than prevented the eventual crisis.
my novel's opening line feels flat: "It was a cold morning in the city." How do I fix it without losing the simplicity?

The line is flat mainly because 'cold morning in the city' is three generic nouns with no specific angle — it could open almost any book. To keep the simplicity but add a hook, anchor it to something sensory-specific or a small tension. For example: "The cold that morning had teeth" (specific, a little unsettling, still short), or "Frost had gotten into the subway grates again, and nobody in the city seemed to mind" (specific detail plus a hint of character/tone — nobody minding implies something about the world). You don't need more words, you need one concrete or odd detail instead of the generic ones.

Yes, it fits — it's still grounded (frost, subway grates are ordinary, physical details) and the 'nobody seemed to mind' clause is a light touch of voice rather than a big tonal swing, so it won't clash with a quiet close-third register. Just make sure the narrator's slightly wry observational tone in that line ('nobody seemed to mind') continues at least a little into the following paragraphs, or the opening will feel like a hook that doesn't match the book.

Funny memory just popped into my head, my grandma used to run legendary garage sales every summer and she'd price everything way higher than it was worth just so people could 'win' by talking her down. Was that actually a smart strategy or just a quirky habit of hers?

That's a genuinely smart, if instinctive, negotiation strategy, and it works on a pretty well-documented psychological principle. When a buyer successfully talks a seller down from an asking price, they leave the interaction feeling like they won something, even if the final price they paid is exactly what a fair, un-negotiated price would have been anyway. People tend to enjoy the process of negotiating almost as much as the outcome, especially in a casual setting like a garage sale where haggling is expected and even part of the fun, so a seller who prices things a bit high isn't just trying to extract more money, they're deliberately creating room for that 'winning' feeling, which tends to make buyers walk away happier and, worth noting, more likely to buy multiple things in one visit or come back to future sales.
Did she risk pricing herself out of sales entirely by starting too high though, or is there basically no downside to that approach at a garage sale specifically?

There's a real risk if the starting price is too far from what anyone believes the item is actually worth, since some buyers will just walk away rather than engage in a negotiation that feels like it's starting from an insultingly high anchor, especially casual browsers who aren't emotionally invested in any particular item and have plenty of other sales to visit that day. The sweet spot tends to be pricing noticeably above what you'd genuinely accept, but not so far above a reasonable estimate of value that it reads as either clueless or greedy. A garage sale context is unusually forgiving of this compared to, say, a retail store, because haggling is a known and expected ritual there, so buyers arrive already anticipating some back and forth, which gives a seller more room to start high without scaring people off than they'd have in a fixed-price setting.
That actually explains why the fixed-price tables at sales always feel a little flat by comparison, now that I think about it.

Exactly, and it's a good observation because it isolates the real mechanism at play, it's not really about the final price at all, it's about whether the buyer got to participate in determining it. A fixed-price table removes that entirely, the transaction becomes purely about whether the listed number seems acceptable, which is a much colder, more purely rational decision with none of the social, game-like texture that makes haggling enjoyable for a lot of people. Interestingly this is part of why some retail contexts that seem to have fixed prices, car dealerships being the classic example, actually build negotiation back into the process deliberately, because sellers have learned that the 'winning' feeling meaningfully increases both satisfaction and the odds of closing a sale, even when the final price ends up landing in roughly the same place a no-haggle price would have.

I have to give a eulogy for my grandfather next week and I've never written one before. I keep freezing up every time I try to start. Any advice on how to even begin?

I'm sorry you're going through this, and freezing up is completely normal, you're trying to write while grieving, which is genuinely one of the harder writing tasks there is, so give yourself grace on the process, not just the outcome. A good way to break the freeze is to stop trying to write "a eulogy" as an abstract genre and instead just start collecting concrete memories, no structure yet, just a messy list: a specific thing he used to say, a smell or place you associate with him, a moment he made you laugh, something he taught you, a small habit or quirk only people who knew him well would recognize. Don't judge these as you write them, quantity over quality at this stage, you're gathering raw material, not composing yet. Once you have eight or ten of these, look for a thread connecting two or three of them, often a value he embodied (generosity, humor, stubbornness in a good way, quiet strength) naturally emerges from the specific memories rather than needing to be stated abstractly from the start. Structure from there: a brief opening (who he was to you, simply stated), two or three of your strongest specific memories organized around that thread, and a closing that speaks either to what he taught you or how he'll be remembered, kept short and sincere rather than trying to summarize an entire life.
How long should it actually be, and is it okay if I get emotional and can't finish reading it smoothly?

Length-wise, 3 to 5 minutes spoken is the typical sweet spot for a eulogy, which translates to roughly 400-700 words depending on your speaking pace, long enough to say something meaningful, short enough that it doesn't become a strain for you or the room to sit through emotionally. If you're nervous about running long while emotional, err shorter rather than longer, a heartfelt 3 minute eulogy lands better than an unfinished 7 minute one you can't get through. And yes, it's entirely okay, honestly expected, to get emotional and need to pause. I just got a pour over setup, a basic dripper and gooseneck kettle, coming from just using a regular drip machine my whole life. My first few attempts have tasted kind of sour and thin. What am I doing wrong?

Sour and thin is a very classic pour over beginner result and it points pretty specifically at under-extraction, meaning the water passed through the grounds without pulling out enough of the coffee's full flavor compounds, generally caused by one or a combination of: grind too coarse, water not hot enough, or total brew time too short. Let's go through the likely fixes in order of impact. Grind size: pour over generally wants a medium-fine grind, similar in texture to coarse sand, if you're using a grind meant for drip machines it might be too coarse for the shorter contact time of manual pour over, try grinding slightly finer and see if the sourness reduces. Water temperature: aim for 195-205F (just off a full boil, let boiled water sit about 30 seconds before pouring), water that's too cool under-extracts and tends toward sour, sharp flavors specifically. Brew time and technique: a standard pour over should take roughly 2.5-3.5 minutes total from first pour to drawdown finishing, if yours is finishing much faster than that, water is flowing through too quickly, which again under-extracts, this connects back to grind size being too coarse most commonly. Try a bloom first too: pour just enough water to saturate the grounds (roughly double the coffee's weight), wait 30-45 seconds for it to bubble and release gas, then continue your normal pour, skipping this step alone commonly causes uneven, under-extracted results.
I don't think I've been doing a bloom at all actually. Walk me through the full pour over process from start to finish with the bloom included?

Here's a full standard process for a typical single-cup pour over, adjust the coffee amount based on your dripper's size, but the ratio guidance holds generally. Start with roughly 1:16 coffee to water ratio by weight, so for a 300g final cup, use about 18-20g of coffee, medium-fine grind. Rinse your paper filter with hot water first if using one (removes papery taste and preheats the dripper), then discard that rinse water and add your grounds, giving the dripper a gentle shake to level the coffee bed. Start your timer and pour just enough hot water (195-205F) to fully saturate all the grounds, roughly 40-50g of water for that 20g of coffee, then stop and let it sit, this is the bloom, wait about 30-45 seconds while you watch it bubble and swell slightly as trapped CO2 releases. After the bloom, begin your main pour in slow, controlled circles, starting from the center and spiraling outward toward the edges then back in, avoiding pouring directly onto the filter's edge, adding water in stages, say pouring up to about half your total water, pausing briefly, then continuing to the full amount, rather than one continuous pour, though a slow continuous spiral works fine too once you're comfortable. Aim for total drawdown time, from first pour to the last water draining through, of about 2.5 to 3.5 minutes. If it finishes faster than that consistently, grind finer next time, if slower, grind slightly coarser, this dial-in process typically takes 3-5 cups of practice before it clicks.

My uncle runs a mid-size family manufacturing business and none of his kids want to take it over, they all went into totally different careers. He's kind of in denial about it. What are families in that situation usually supposed to do?

That situation is extremely common, actually, estimates vary but a large share of family businesses never successfully pass to a next generation for exactly this reason, interests and career paths diverging, so your uncle is far from alone even if it feels like a uniquely painful problem within his own family. The families that navigate it best tend to separate two questions that often get tangled together emotionally, whether the business itself should continue existing in some form, and whether it specifically needs to stay in the family's hands to do so. Once those get separated, several real options open up that don't require a reluctant child to take over against their wishes, bringing in an outside professional manager to run day-to-day operations while the family retains ownership and a board-level role, selling to another company in the same industry, or arranging an employee-led buyout where longtime trusted managers take over operational control, sometimes with family members staying on as passive owners collecting a share of profits rather than running things themselves.
The employee buyout idea is interesting, has that actually worked well in practice for other family businesses, or does it usually fall apart?

It has a genuinely mixed track record, and the difference between the ones that work and the ones that fall apart tends to come down to how early the planning starts and how realistic the valuation and financing structure are. The ones that go well typically begin the transition years in advance, giving the incoming employee-owners time to build up both the operational confidence and, just as importantly, the financial capacity to actually buy in gradually rather than needing to come up with the full purchase price all at once, sometimes structured so the departing family takes payments over time rather than one lump sum, which also has the side benefit of keeping the outgoing owner financially invested in the company's continued success rather than walking away indifferent to what happens next. The ones that fall apart tend to rush the timeline, often because the triggering event is the owner's sudden health issue or unplanned retirement rather than deliberate planning, and the new owners end up over-leveraged or under-prepared for the parts of running a business that a longtime owner-family had absorbed informally over decades without ever writing it down anywhere.

That point about knowledge never being written down really resonates, my uncle definitely runs things by instinct with 40 years of relationships in his head. Is there anything a family can realistically do about that specific problem before a transition happens?

Yes, and it's honestly one of the more tractable parts of succession planning precisely because it doesn't require resolving the emotionally fraught ownership question first, it can start well before anyone has decided who, if anyone, takes over. The practical approach is treating the owner's undocumented knowledge as a project in itself, systematically capturing the relationships, informal processes, and judgment calls that exist only in his head, who the key suppliers and customers actually are and what makes each relationship work, which decisions he makes on gut feel that could be turned into at least a rough documented guideline, which employees quietly hold critical institutional knowledge themselves that nobody has ever asked to write anything down. Bringing in even a junior operations hire specifically tasked with shadowing him and documenting this over a year or two, well before any ownership transition is finalized, dramatically de-risks whatever the eventual outcome turns out to be, whether that's a family member stepping in after all, an employee buyout, or an outside sale, since a business that isn't entirely dependent on one person's memory is more resilient and, frankly, more valuable under any of those paths.

why is binary search O(log n) instead of O(n)? I get that it halves the array but I want the intuition for why that gives log n

The key intuition is thinking about how many times you can cut something in half before it's down to one element. If you start with n elements and halve the search space each step, after k steps you have roughly n divided by 2 to the k elements left. The search ends when that quantity reaches 1, which happens when 2 to the k equals n, meaning k equals log base 2 of n. So the number of halving steps grows proportionally to the logarithm of n rather than n itself. A concrete way to feel it: for a list of a million elements, log2(1,000,000) is only about 20, so binary search finds anything in about 20 comparisons max, compared to potentially a million comparisons for a linear scan.
does that mean doubling the input size only adds one more comparison on average?

Pretty much, yes, for the worst case at least. If you double n, log2(2n) equals log2(n) plus log2(2), which is just log2(n) plus 1. So doubling the array size only ever adds one additional halving step in the worst case, which is exactly why binary search scales so gracefully compared to linear-time algorithms as datasets grow large.

what's the difference between a transform boundary and the other two plate boundary types?

There are three main types based on how plates move relative to each other. Divergent boundaries are where plates move apart, allowing magma to rise and create new crust, like at mid-ocean ridges. Convergent boundaries are where plates move toward each other, which can result in one plate subducting beneath another, forming deep trenches and volcanic arcs, or in two continental plates colliding to push up mountain ranges like the Himalayas. Transform boundaries are different from both because the plates aren't moving apart or together at all, they're sliding horizontally past each other, and crust is neither created nor destroyed at this type of boundary. The San Andreas Fault in California is the classic transform boundary example, where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other laterally, producing frequent earthquakes from the friction and stress buildup rather than volcanic activity.
why don't transform boundaries produce volcanoes the way convergent ones do?

Volcanism at convergent boundaries is driven by subduction - one plate gets forced down into the mantle, and the intense heat and pressure cause water and other volatiles carried down with the subducting plate to lower the melting point of the overlying mantle rock, generating magma that rises to the surface. Transform boundaries don't involve any plate being pushed down into the mantle or any new material rising up to fill a gap, since the plates are just sliding past each other laterally with no vertical component of motion. Without that subduction process or the upwelling that happens at divergent boundaries, there's no mechanism generating fresh magma, so transform boundaries produce lots of seismic stress and earthquakes but essentially no volcanic activity.

what's the actual difference between a 9th chord and an add9 chord?

A 9th chord implies the full stack built from the root: root, third, fifth, flat or natural seventh, and the ninth on top - so it's essentially a seventh chord with the ninth added. An add9 chord skips the seventh entirely - it's just a triad (root, third, fifth) with the ninth added directly on top, no seventh involved. So a C9 chord would be C-E-G-Bb-D, while a Cadd9 would be C-E-G-D, with no Bb at all. The sonic difference is notable - the add9 has a cleaner, more open sound since it avoids the tension of the seventh, and it's common in pop and folk voicings, while proper 9th chords show up a lot more in jazz where that seventh's tension is part of the desired color.

It's a favorite closing or coloring chord in jazz and lounge styles because it has a warm, resolved quality without the harmonic pull that a seventh would create, since there's no leading-tone tension pushing it toward another chord.

I'm writing a fantasy novel and my villain currently just feels like generic "wants power for power's sake" evil. How do I make him feel like a real, three dimensional character instead of a cardboard cutout?

The fastest fix for a generic power-hungry villain is usually giving him a goal that's actually sympathetic or at least internally coherent from his own point of view, since the flattest villains are the ones who exist purely as an obstacle for the hero, with wanting-power-for-its-own-sake being basically the laziest version of this, it explains nothing about why he specifically wants it or what he'd actually do with it once achieved. Every genuinely compelling villain, think Killmonger, Thanos, even Darth Vader by the prequels, has a version of events in which they are the protagonist and their actions are justified, often even noble, from inside their own logic, the reader or viewer just happens to disagree with their methods or their read on the situation, not necessarily with their underlying goal. Ask yourself: what does your villain believe is broken about the world, and what personal history convinced him of that belief? Maybe he watched a previous ruler's weakness or mercy directly cause a tragedy, and now genuinely believes that strength and control, even brutal control, prevents worse suffering than kindness ever could, that's a coherent worldview a reader can understand even while rooting against him. Give him a moment, even a small one, of genuine care, humor, or vulnerability directed at someone, a loyal subordinate, a memory of someone he lost, since villains who are capable of real feeling toward at least one person read as far more human and threatening than ones who are cruel indiscriminately to everyone including their own allies.
That's helpful. Should his worldview actually be partially correct, like should the hero have to admit he has a point about something?

Yes, and this is often what separates a good villain from a great one, giving him a piece of truth the hero has to genuinely reckon with, rather than a worldview that's simply wrong and eventually disproven by the plot, creates real thematic tension that elevates the whole story beyond a straightforward good-versus-evil structure. The key craft element here is being precise about which part of his worldview is right and which part is wrong, since making him entirely correct risks making the hero's opposition feel arbitrary or even wrong-headed, while making him entirely incorrect just recreates the flat villain problem you started with in a slightly more dressed up form. A common and effective structure: the villain correctly diagnoses a real problem (say, the previous ruling system truly was corrupt, or truly did fail vulnerable people, or truly was too slow and indecisive to prevent tragedy) but proposes a solution that trades that problem for a worse one (order bought through fear and control that ultimately causes more suffering than the disorder it replaced, or protection that comes at the cost of everyone's freedom or individuality). This lets your hero, and your reader, sit with genuine discomfort, agreeing with the villain's critique of the world while still rejecting his prescription for fixing it, which is a much more interesting position than simple moral clarity. Practically, look for at least one scene where the hero has no good rebuttal in the moment, maybe they change the subject, or deflect, or simply say "there has to be another way" without being able to fully articulate what that way is yet, since a hero who can perfectly counter every villain argument makes the villain retroactively seem less threatening intellectually, while one who's genuinely rattled by a point makes the philosophical conflict feel real and high stakes rather than a foregone conclusion.

why do so many greek myths have gods punishing mortals for things that seem kind of minor, like Arachne just being good at weaving?

A lot of those stories are really about the concept of hubris - excessive pride or self-elevation to a level that challenges the gods' status. Arachne's offense wasn't just skill, it was boasting that her weaving surpassed Athena's and refusing to show any deference when challenged, which in the Greek moral framework was a direct assault on the natural hierarchy between mortals and gods. These myths functioned partly as cultural teaching tools reinforcing the idea that mortal excellence should be paired with humility, and that overstepping your bounds relative to divine authority invited disaster regardless of how justified your confidence seemed. It's a recurring pattern - Niobe boasting about her many children compared to Leto's two, Marsyas challenging Apollo to a musical contest - the specific talent varies but the punished trait is almost always the same overreach.

In everyday Athenian legal and social life, things like murder or theft were obviously treated as serious crimes with real legal consequences. But myths operated on a different register, dealing with cosmic order and the gods' prerogatives rather than civic law, so hubris against divine authority got dramatized as uniquely catastrophic because it threatened the symbolic order the myths were built to reinforce, even though in practical terms Greek society clearly punished violent crimes severely too.

I've been playing guitar for about 8 months, mostly self taught. I can do basic chords and simple strumming but I feel stuck. What should a practice routine actually look like to break through a plateau like this?

Plateaus at the 6-12 month mark are extremely common and usually come from practicing broadly (playing songs you already sort of know) rather than deliberately (targeting specific weak points), so the fix is restructuring practice time into distinct blocks rather than just "playing guitar" for however long. A solid 30-45 minute daily routine at your stage: 5-10 minutes of warmup, chromatic exercises or simple scale runs to build finger independence and speed without thinking about a song. 10 minutes of chord transition drills, picking your two or three worst chord changes (commonly F, B minor, or barre chords generally) and looping just that transition slowly with a metronome, gradually increasing speed only once it's clean. 10-15 minutes of strumming pattern work, deliberately practicing patterns slightly harder than what you use in songs, including syncopation and muting, since strumming feels stuck when it isn't pushed past comfort level. The remaining time on actual songs, but pick one slightly above your comfort level rather than only songs you can already play, since that's where real progress happens. Also record yourself weekly, it's uncomfortable but genuinely the fastest way to notice timing and buzzing issues you can't hear while playing.
Barre chords are definitely my weak point, I basically avoid them. Any specific tips there?

Barre chords are the single most common wall at this stage, and it's almost always a technique issue rather than a strength issue, even though it feels like you just need stronger hands. The biggest fix is thumb position: your thumb should be roughly behind your index finger on the back of the neck, not wrapped over the top, and pushing more with thumb-to-finger squeeze rather than raw finger pressure into the fretboard reduces the effort dramatically. Second, angle the barre finger slightly, using the side of the finger rather than the flat pad, since the side has a harder bone edge that presses strings down more efficiently with less muscle effort. Third, isolate practice: don't practice barre chords inside full songs yet, instead just fret an E-shape barre chord anywhere on the neck, strum once, release completely, rest, and repeat, focusing purely on getting a clean sound with minimal buzzing, maybe 5 minutes a day of just this. Your hand also needs actual physical adaptation time, calluses and small hand muscles genuinely get stronger over 2-4 weeks of consistent short practice, so don't judge progress day to day, judge it week to week. Once a single barre chord rings clean consistently, add slow chord changes into and out of it before ever trying it inside a real song at tempo.

why would anyone use quicksort over mergesort if quicksort's worst case is O(n^2)?

In practice quicksort tends to be faster on average despite that worst-case risk, mainly because of constant factors and memory behavior. Quicksort sorts in place, needing only O(log n) additional space for the recursion stack, while mergesort needs O(n) additional space for the merge step, which matters a lot for large datasets or memory-constrained environments. Quicksort also tends to have better cache locality since it works on contiguous subarrays in place, while mergesort's merge step involves more scattered memory access patterns in some implementations. The O(n^2) worst case for quicksort happens specifically with poor pivot choices, like always picking the first or last element on already-sorted or adversarially constructed input, but with randomized pivot selection or median-of-three pivoting, that worst case becomes extremely unlikely in practice, so most real-world implementations, including many standard library sort functions, use quicksort or a hybrid approach as the default.
so what do actual standard library implementations use these days?

Most modern standard libraries use hybrid approaches rather than a pure textbook algorithm. Many use introsort, which starts with quicksort but switches to heapsort if the recursion depth exceeds a threshold, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case while keeping quicksort's typical average-case speed. For small subarrays, many implementations switch to insertion sort since it has lower constant overhead for small n. Python's built-in sort, Timsort, is a different hybrid entirely, designed around merge sort and insertion sort specifically to exploit existing runs of ordered data common in real-world data, which mergesort and quicksort don't inherently take advantage of.
